messages.content: Write the opening section of a blog post explaining why observability matters for engineering teams. Around 250 words.

## Nobody Wants Dashboards

The pager goes off at 2:14 a.m. Checkout is failing for some customers — not all of them, and nobody can say which ones. You open the dashboard your team built last quarter. CPU: fine. Memory: fine. Request rate: normal-ish. Error rate up, from 0.1% to 0.4%. Great. Now what?

That gap, between knowing something is wrong and knowing *what* is wrong, is where teams burn their nights. It's also the only thing observability is for. The rest is vocabulary.

Monitoring answers questions you thought to ask in advance. You predicted the disk would fill, so you graphed the disk. Observability is what you have when the question is one nobody anticipated: why do checkout failures cluster on requests that went through the new payment retry path, but only for accounts created before last month's schema migration? You can't pre-build a panel for that. You can only build a system where the data is rich enough to ask.

The difference shows up in numbers most teams never publish. Time to detect. Time to name the failing component. How many engineers get pulled out of bed before the right one is found. I've watched a team drop mean time to resolution from 90 minutes to under 15 without touching a line of application logic — they changed what their logs carried.

So this post isn't about picking a vendor. It's about what your systems can tell you on the night you don't already know the answer.

~255 words. One thing to swap: the 90 → 15 minute anecdote is a stand-in — replace it with a real number from your own incident history, or cut the sentence, since a made-up specific is worse than none.
Rewrite the text above. Keep the same length and the same purpose. Return only the rewritten text.
